articles.title: Philanthropy’s biggest failure is its fear of failure
As slow as an India-US trade deal
articles.summary: There are forces who have probably been assigned the task of ensuring that Marco Rubio doesn't overhear this during the next few days he's here in India. But India is a big and loud place, and this corner column only mirrors it. So, consider our duty to put on record a new idiomatic phrase in English that has gained traction over the last few months: 'As slow as an India-US trade deal'.Those familiar with formulations such as 'watching paint dry' and 'waiting for Godot' may already know what we're talking about. Except, this latest idiom describes an activity that is simultaneously happening, not happening, and about to happen.Its most remarkable feature is its elasticity. A delayed flight is merely late. A delayed marriage may be called off. But something proceeding 'as slow as an India-US trade deal' enjoys permanent forward momentum without the inconvenience of arriving.Whenever an official announces that negotiations are 'almost complete', seasoned observers understand that it's nudge-nudge, wink-wink for another postponement. 'We are very close' means further away than previously feared. 'Final stages' suggests the beginning of another round. 'Constructive discussions' indicates that nobody has thrown a chair. Trade negotiators on both sides of the Indo-Pacific water table have finally produced something of lasting value: a phrase.

articles.title: France: Curfews bring calm to Paris
articles.summary: PARIS: Paris returned to calm on Tuesday after its first quiet night since a weekend marred by France's most destructive rioting in years, as authorities imposed curfews in several cities in an effort to prevent another round of rioting and looting.At least 2,400 people were arrested after rioters in cities across France on Saturday clashed with police, set cars on fire, stormed public buildings and engulfed a historic city hall in flames, during nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.On Sunday evening, small groups set fire to trash bins, bicycles and other objects in the streets and looted businesses in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and other cities.Also Read: Paris police issue overnight curfew in 2 areas of French capital to try to prevent further disorderIn the capital, a curfew ran from 11 p.m. on Monday to 6 a.m. Tuesday, and a police helicopter circled over Place de la Republique overnight, a central point in the weekend clashes, sweeping the square with a searchlight to check that the order was being respected.Early Tuesday morning, workers used a crane to remove a giant fluorescent yellow vest draped over the statue at the center of the square, a reference to the " yellow vest " protests over fuel prices that began in 2018 and shook the first term of President Emmanuel Macron.Workers then used pressure washers to blast graffiti off the monument."The targeted curfews helped keep last night calm," Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu wrote on X on Tuesday, adding that new curfews would be imposed that night "wherever the situation requires," decided locally by prefects, the state's representatives in each region, together with mayors.Speaking in Lille, northern France, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said 149 people had been jailed nationwide as of Tuesday at noon. According to the Justice Ministry, of the roughly 2,500 people arrested since Saturday, more than 800 have been sent before prosecutors, most of whom were either put on trial immediately or ordered to appear at a later hearing.In Paris alone, about 300 people have been sent before prosecutors following the Oct. 17 protests, the city prosecutor's office said in a statement.Darmanin said he asked prosecutors to appeal any sentence they considered too lenient. "People with no criminal record ending up in prison for property crimes is extremely rare, if not unheard of," he said, arguing that the French justice system will be "extremely firm."In Lille, he said, three men aged 20 to 25 with no criminal record were each sentenced to 10 months in prison and imprisoned immediately for looting a video game store in the city's old town.The National Assembly, France's lower house of parliament, is launching an inquiry into the Oct. 17 violence and the authorities' policing strategy, its speaker, Yael Braun-Pivet, said, with findings expected "by the end of the year."

articles.title: Giant 'heat storms' are scorching the Earth
articles.summary: By Maurice Tamman, Ben Welsh, Pete Mckenzie, Charlie Szymanski, Delgerzaya Delgerjargal, Robbie Corey-Boulet, Loucoumane Coulibaly, Jeff Horwitz and Joan FausIn less than a lifetime, about six and a half decades, heat waves have evolved from sporadic, isolated episodes to massive, cascading weather events that can blanket vast swaths of the planet for months or even years at a time.The largest heat wave of the 1960s reached about 6% of the planet as it drifted for 46 days over the Atlantic Ocean, parts of Latin America and West Africa.The largest one this decade swept across almost 85% of the globe during its 367-day lifetime, stretching into the polar latitudes and touching virtually every human being on Earth.To continue calling such sprawling phenomena "heat waves" would be like calling a monsoon a rain shower. To understand the new reality of these immense expanses of heat, Reuters consulted with two dozen meteorologists and climate researchers - and analyzed temperatures for every hour of every day since 1960 for more than one million grid squares covering the entire globe. Out of those results we developed a new concept: the "heat storm."Simply put, heat storms are supersized heat waves. Reuters uses a conservative benchmark to define an ordinary heat wave: five or more consecutive days of abnormally high temperatures. Then we define the largest heat waves - those that at their peak cover at least 1% of the globe, roughly half the size of Canada - as heat storms.Applying this definition, Reuters identified a startling transformation. Heat storms were rare in the 1960s, when they averaged about five active storms per year. This decade, heat storms have swarmed the planet, averaging about 102 a year.One of them caused this summer's deadly heat in Europe, notching the highest June temperatures ever recorded in Bordeaux, Budapest, and Bilbao, the latter of which hit 42.7 degrees Celsius (108.9 degrees Fahrenheit). Roasting Europe for most of June and July, the heat storm warped steel railroad tracks, drove what European governments estimated were more than 10,000 excess deaths in a single week, and prompted Belgian zookeepers to cool their tigers by feeding them raw meat encased in ice.The largest heat storm on record - the one that lasted for 367 days over 2023-2024 and reached almost 85% of the globe - sent temperatures in parts of the Philippines up to 38 C (100.5 F), immiserating students in the country's mostly unairconditioned schools. In Manila, math teacher Joel Arrojado recalled a student who was face-down at his desk, crying. When Arrojado coaxed the boy into looking up, Arrojado saw his face and chest covered in blood. The boy, Arrojado said, had suffered a spontaneous nosebleed, a common problem in extreme heat. "Heat is the biggest killer from climate change," he said, noting that it can lead to "famine, hunger, death, conflict over resources."A NEW WAY TO UNDERSTAND CLIMATE CHANGEHeat storms constitute a new way to conceptualize how Earth's climate is changing as humanity pumps greenhouse gases into the atmosphere.The determination by climatologists that the average global temperature in 2025 was 1.47 C (2.6 F) above the pre-industrial level is useful to scientists and policymakers, but to many people it's so abstract as to be meaningless. articles.summary: Leh: In a historic milestone for the administration of justice in the Union Territory of Ladakh, Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant, on Sunday, inaugurated the newly established Ladakh Bench of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh at Melongthang, Leh.The establishment of the Bench marks a significant step towards bringing justice closer to the people of Ladakh, particularly those residing in remote and far-flung areas, by reducing the hardships, time and expenditure involved in travelling to Srinagar or Jammu for judicial proceedings.Also read: Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council Kargil chief to seek dissolution, likely to join BJPThe dais was graced by CJI Surya Kant; Justice M M Sundresh, Justice P S Narasimha and Justice Arun Palli, Judges of the Supreme Court of India; R Venkataramani, Attorney General of India; Vinai Kumar Saxena, Lieutenant Governor of Ladakh; Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati, Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh; Justice Sanjeev Kumar, Justice Sindhu Sharma and Justice Rajnesh Oswal, Judges of the High Court; and Ashish Kumar Kundra, Chief Secretary, Union Territory of Ladakh.The occasion was further graced by Justice Tashi Rabstan, former Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh; all the Judges of the High Court, accompanied by their spouses; the Director General of Police, Law Secretary, Administrative Secretaries and senior officers of the army, civil administration, police and other departments of the Union Territory of Ladakh.Officers of the High Court Registry, headed by MK Sharma, Registrar General, Additional Solicitors General of India (ASGIs), Deputy Solicitors General of India (DSGIs) and Presidents of the Bar Associations of Leh and Kargil also attended the ceremony.Upon his arrival, the CJI was accorded a ceremonial Guard of Honour, following which he unveiled the inauguration plaque. A group photograph was taken, followed by a guided tour of the Court Complex. The formal proceedings commenced with the National Song and National Anthem, followed by a welcome address by Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati, Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.In his address, Bhati emphasised that access to justice had been the guiding principle behind the establishment of the Ladakh Bench. He observed that, under the visionary leadership of the CJI, the establishment of a constitutional Court in one of the highest-altitude regions of the world marked a historic milestone in bringing justice closer to the people, particularly those residing in remote and geographically challenging areas of Ladakh.The CJI also virtually inaugurated the Green Wall, symbolising the judiciary's commitment to environmental conservation. The initiative was marked by the presentation of planters to the dignitaries and screening of a short video. In his special address, Vinai Kumar Saxena, Lieutenant Governor of Ladakh, termed the establishment of the Ladakh Bench a historic milestone in strengthening access to justice in the region. He also highlighted the significance of the Green Wall initiative in promoting environmental conservation and ecological sustainability in Ladakh.Justice MM Sundresh, Justice P S Narasimha and Justice Arun Palli, Judges of the Supreme Court of India, and R Venkataramani, Attorney General of India, also addressed the gathering on the occasion.A major highlight of the ceremony was the launch of four significant initiatives by the Chief Justice of India, comprising the Green Wall and digital initiatives, namely, the e-Filing Portal and Document Management System (DMS) for the Ladakh Bench and the Online Recruitment Portal of the High Court.The e-Filing Portal will enable advocates and litigants, particularly those from remote areas, to file cases electronically without travelling to the Court, while the DMS will facilitate digital management of judicial records. The Online Recruitment Portal will streamline recruitment in the High Court and District Judiciary, promoting transparency, accessibility and efficiency.Significantly, the Ladakh Bench shall function as a fully IT-enabled, paperless Court, equipped with modern digital infrastructure. The Court Complex also houses a dedicated Digitisation Centre, Filing Counter, Bar Room, Litigants' Sitting Area, Conference Room and Video Conferencing (VC) Room, ensuring efficient and technology-driven judicial functioning.The CJI Surya Kant also initiated work for the installation of solar power systems at 11 locations, reinforcing the judiciary's commitment to renewable energy and sustainable infrastructure.Also read: Ladakh integral to India, China's denial can't change facts: MEAIn his Presidential address, the CJI emphasised the role of technology and legal aid in ensuring access to justice in Ladakh and appreciated the e-Initiatives launched to overcome geographical barriers.The programme concluded with a vote of thanks by Ashish Kundra, Chief Secretary, Union Territory of Ladakh, followed by the National Song and National Anthem.The inauguration of the Ladakh Bench, together with the launch of digital and infrastructure initiatives, heralds a new chapter in the judicial history of Ladakh, reaffirming the judiciary's commitment to accessible, efficient, technology-enabled and citizen-centric justice, while ensuring that geographical distances and difficult terrain do not become barriers to the administration of justice.
